items.title: A volcano in Tonga exploded so loudly in 2022 that people in Alaska, 6,000 miles away, were woken by the booms. Hawaii, at half that distance, heard nothing at all
items.summary: When heavy booms woke Iris Caldentey in Palmer, Alaska, she went outside to check whether someone was breaking into the family’s cars. In Unalaska, Laresa Syverson initially blamed her cat. The real source was Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai, nearly 10 000 km (6 200 miles) away—even though much closer Hawai‘i reported no audible sound. items.title: Famous New Mexico rock formation destroyed after torrential El Niño rains
items.summary: Officials expected to investigate whether super El Niño storms in US south-west damaged the Alien Throne spires Undulating, gravity-defying rock spires are one of the most magical parts of the landscape of the US south-west. But after torrential rainstorms linked to the super El Niño season, at least one famous rock formation in north-west New Mexico has been found in pieces. Continue reading...

items.title: In 2002 a magnitude 7.9 quake on the Denali Fault shoved the ground about 14 feet sideways under the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, but engineers had designed Teflon sliders for the pipe nearly 30 years earlier, and no oil spilled.
items.summary: On November 3, 2002, the M7.9 Denali Fault earthquake ruptured about 340 km (211 miles) of central Alaska and displaced the ground beneath the Trans-Alaska Pipeline by roughly 4.3–5.8 m (14–19 feet), depending on how the distributed rupture is measured. The pipe slid across low-friction supports and flexed through its zigzag alignment; it did not rupture and no oil escaped. Source

items.title: Kīlauea episode 56 ends abruptly after nearly 6 hours of lava fountaining, Hawaii
items.summary: Episode 56 of Kīlauea’s ongoing Halemaʻumaʻu eruption began at 12:10 HST (22:10 UTC) on November 5, 2026, and ended abruptly at 18:01 HST that day (04:01 UTC on November 6) after nearly six hours of continuous lava fountaining. Fountains reached about 200 m (660 feet), while the eruption plume rose to 5 500 m (18 000 feet) above sea level. Source
